**Important note:** this week's examples include a commercial product
and two platforms. Where I say what a company did, the source is the
paper or the company's own statement, linked. Where I say what it
should have done, the view is mine, and a well-argued position I think
is wrong can still get full marks.

## Summary

A score is a number computed about a person and used to decide
something about them. The number measures one thing, $Y$, and is taken
to stand for another, $Y^\star$. The two come apart in three ways:
noise, an offset that differs between groups, and a response by the
people being measured. A health system's risk score measured next year's
medical cost and was taken to stand for how ill a patient was; at the
same cost, Black patients were sicker, so the score flagged fewer of
them for extra care, and the ones it did flag were sicker than the
White patients it flagged. In a model with an offset $\beta_A$ for one group, selecting above a
threshold $t$ on the measure is selecting above $t - \beta_A$ on the thing
measured, for that group only.

Once a score is rewarded, the people and systems it is applied to act
on the score. That changes the equation for $Y$, an intervention, and
what $Y$ says about $Y^\star$ afterward is not what it said before.
Strategic classification and performative prediction are two formal
versions of this. Reinforcement learning says the same thing in other
letters: an agent is given a reward $R$, and the good we care about is
a utility $U$.


::: {.cell}

:::


## Scores

### Citation counts

Week 1 followed studies through one filter: of the tests that were run,
the ones with $p < 0.05$ were the ones that reached print. The same
filter operates further down the pipeline. De Vries and colleagues
(2018) took 105 trials of antidepressants that drug companies had
registered with the US Food and Drug Administration, which classified
53 as positive and 52 as negative or questionable, and followed them
into the literature.

![](../../files/devries_2018_fig1.png){fig-align="center" width="85%"}

Of the 105 trials, 77 were published: 98% of the positive trials and
48% of the negative ones. Ten negative trials appeared positive in
print after an unfavorable outcome was dropped or a secondary outcome
promoted to primary. Of the 77 published, 4 said plainly that the drug
had not beaten placebo. And in the literature as cited, positive trials
were cited about three times as often as negative ones, 92 citations
to 32 on average. Each panel is a selection, and each selection runs
the same way. The file-drawer effect turns variance into bias.

A citation count is a score. It is what a researcher's output is
measured by, and it is taken to stand for a contribution to knowledge.
The figure shows the two coming apart stage by stage: at each stage,
more of the positive results survive. The paper documents the
selections; it says nothing about anyone's intentions.

### What a score does to the people it is applied to

The citation count also does something to the people it measures. A
researcher who knows that positive results are published and cited has
a reason to find one, and week 1's p-hacking loop is a way of finding
one. Last week's lecture put it in one sentence: what a score does to
the people who write for it is a different mechanism from selection.

The usual name for this is **Goodhart's law**. Charles Goodhart, in a
1975 paper on monetary management in the United Kingdom, wrote that
"Any observed statistical regularity will tend to collapse once
pressure is placed upon it for control purposes." The quotation is the
one the [Wikipedia article](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Goodhart%27s_law&oldid=1379318143) you were asked to skim
gives, from the paper's 1981 reprint, page 116; the paper itself was
not available to check. The wording most people know is Marilyn
Strathern's, from a 1997 paper on auditing British universities: "When
a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure" (Strathern
1997, p. 308).

Manheim and Garrabrant (2018) sort the ways this happens into four.
Their *regressional* case is the one the next section derives: a proxy
that is the goal plus noise overstates the goal wherever the proxy is
large. Their *adversarial* case is the one the section on systems that
adapt takes up: once the measure is rewarded, other people, with aims
of their own, act on it. In their *causal* case the regulator's own
intervention on the proxy changes its relation to the goal, and in
their *extremal* case an optimizer pushes the system into a region
where the old relation does not hold; both are named here and not
developed.

### Measured and intended

Write $Y$ for the outcome a system measures and $Y^\star$ for the one
it was meant to measure: the one we would use if we could. In a
regression $Y$ is the response; in a classifier it is the label; in a
reward signal it is the number the agent is given.

| $Y$, measured | $Y^\star$, intended |
|:---|:---|
| citations | contribution to knowledge |
| $p < 0.05$ | a true effect |
| a job center's placement rate | people in work because of it |
| a patient's medical cost | how ill the patient is |
| a video's views | a viewer informed, or entertained, on their own terms |

The two differ by three routes, and the rest of these notes take them
in turn.

1. **Noise.** $Y = Y^\star + \varepsilon$, with $\varepsilon$
   unrelated to anything else. A noisy measure is still right on
   average, but a slope on it is flattened toward zero.
2. **An offset that differs between groups.**
   $Y = Y^\star + \beta_A A$, with $A$ a group and $\beta_A \ne 0$. The measure is
   right on average for one group and off by $\beta_A$ for the other, and
   selecting on it selects the groups differently.
3. **A response to being measured.** Once $Y$ is rewarded, the people
   and systems it is applied to act on $Y$ itself. The equation for
   $Y$ changes.

The first lens asks about every row of the table: what are we
optimizing or predicting? The answer "cost" or "views" is correct and
incomplete. The next question is what the number was taken to stand
for, and who decided that it could.

## Cost as a proxy for need

### A risk score in health care

Obermeyer, Powers, Vogeli and Mullainathan (2019) studied a commercial
risk score at a large academic hospital. The score was used to decide
which patients were offered extra care. Patients above the 97th
percentile of the score were identified for a care-management program
automatically; patients above the 55th were flagged to their doctor.
Whether an identified patient was then enrolled was a decision for
clinicians, so the paper's numbers are about identification, and these
notes say "selected" for it. The score was a
prediction of each patient's **medical costs** in the coming year, and
race was not one of its inputs. By industry estimates, the authors
write, tools of this class are applied to roughly 200 million people in
the United States each year.

The sample was patients in primary care at the hospital from 2013 to
2015: 6,079 Black patients and 43,539 White patients, counted over
11,929 and 88,080 patient-years. A patient-year is one patient's data
for one calendar year. The authors could see each patient's score and
their health records.

At a given score, Black and White patients cost about the same in the
following year, which is what a cost model should deliver. At a given
score, Black patients were sicker. The paper's Figure 1A plots the
number of active chronic conditions against the score's percentile,
one curve per group, and the paper reports that at the same score
Black patients had more illness. At the 97th percentile, the automatic-enrollment point,
Black patients averaged 4.8 active chronic conditions and White
patients 3.8, 26% more.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](notes_files/figure-html/obermeyer_curves-1.png){fig-alt='Two rising curves of active chronic conditions against risk-score percentile, the Black patients\' curve above the White patients\' at every percentile; at the dashed 97th-percentile line the curves are labeled 4.8 and 3.8.' width=576}
:::
:::


Why? At the same number of chronic conditions, Black patients in the
sample generated about $1,801 less in medical costs a year, and
everyone in the sample was insured. The authors name two routes.
Barriers to care: poverty, geography, transport, the demands of work
and child care, and knowing when to seek care, all of which reduce
spending at a given level of illness. And the effect of race on the
care a patient receives once they are seen; the paper cites a trial
(its reference 32) that found higher uptake of recommended preventive
care when the doctor was Black.
Either way, cost measures need with an offset that depends on race.

The authors simulate what removing the gap would do. The share of Black
patients among those identified automatically would rise from 17.7% to
46.5%. Separately,
they trained new models on three labels. With total cost as the label,
Black patients were 14.1% of the highest-risk group (the 97th
percentile and above); with avoidable cost, 21.0%; with the number of
active chronic conditions, 26.7%. The label is the choice, and the
paper is about what that one choice did.

The paper's abstract describes the first figure as "the percentage of
Black patients receiving additional help," which is not what was
computed; the body gives the Black share of patients auto-identified
at the 97th percentile. A paper about a loosely specified target whose
abstract loosely specifies its own number is the first lens applied to
the paper that teaches it. Read the body.

### A model: an offset for one group

Take need $Y^\star$ to have the same distribution in both groups (an assumption, not a finding: see below), and
let $A = 1$ for one group and $0$ for the other. The measure is
$$
Y = Y^\star + \beta_A A ,
$$
and the program selects everyone with $Y > t$. For group $0$ that is
$Y^\star > t$. For group $1$ it is $Y^\star + \beta_A > t$, or
$Y^\star > t - \beta_A$. **An offset of $\beta_A$ in the measure is a threshold
moved by $-\beta_A$ for that group.** With $\beta_A < 0$, as in the paper, group
$1$ has to be iller to be selected.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](notes_files/figure-html/offset_densities-1.png){fig-alt='Two normal curves of the measure Y, the group-1 curve shifted left by half a standard deviation, with the threshold t drawn as a dashed line and the two tails above it shaded.' width=576}
:::
:::


Two things follow, and both are in the paper's data.

**Who is selected.** Group $1$ is selected with probability
$P(Y^\star > t - \beta_A)$ and group $0$ with probability $P(Y^\star > t)$.
With $Y^\star \sim N(0, 1)$ and $t$ the 97th percentile, $t = 1.88$:

| offset $\beta_A$ | selected, group 0 | selected, group 1 | ratio | mean need of selected in group 0 | mean need of selected in group 1 |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 0.0 | 3.0% | 3.0% | 1.00 | 2.27 | 2.27 |
| -0.5 | 3.0% | 0.9% | 0.29 | 2.27 | 2.71 |
| -1.0 | 3.0% | 0.2% | 0.07 | 2.27 | 3.17 |

An offset of half a standard deviation cuts group $1$'s chance of
selection to less than a third of group $0$'s. In percentage points
the gap is small, 3.0 against 0.9; at the median the same offset would
move the shares from 50% to 31%, a gap of 19 points but a ratio of only
0.62. A threshold in the tail turns a small offset into a large
proportional disparity, because the normal density falls quickly there.

**How ill the selected are.** The mean of a standard normal variable
given that it exceeds $z$ is
$$
E[Y^\star \mid Y^\star > z] = \frac{\phi(z)}{1 - \Phi(z)} ,
$$
the inverse Mills ratio from week 1, where it gave the expected size of
an estimate that survived the significance filter. Here it gives the
mean need of the selected in each group: $z = t$ for group $0$ and
$z = t - \beta_A$ for group $1$. Since the ratio increases in $z$, the
selected members of group $1$ are iller on average than the selected
members of group $0$, by about half a standard deviation in the second
row of the table.

The paper's Figure 1A compares a different quantity: need at a given
score, not above a threshold. In this model that comparison is
simpler. Two patients with the same measure $Y = y$ have needs $y$ and
$y - \beta_A$, so at every score group $1$ is iller by $-\beta_A$, and the gap does
not depend on where the threshold is. The table's comparison, among
the selected, adds the tail effect on top: group $1$'s selected members
are drawn from further out in the need distribution.

This is a bias, and more data does not touch it. A larger sample
estimates the offset more precisely and selects the same people.

The model assumes need has the same distribution in both groups. In
the paper's sample it does not (Black patients were on average sicker),
which is why the paper's shares are what they are rather than the
table's; the direction of both effects is the same. The model also
assumes the offset is the same for everyone in group $1$, when in the
paper it comes from barriers that vary from person to person. Read the
table as a mechanism, not as the hospital's numbers.

### Who bears the error

A threshold makes two kinds of mistake. A patient can be selected
without needing the program, which uses a place and the program's
time. A patient can be left out while needing it, which costs the
patient. Setting $t$ at the 97th percentile rather than the 90th trades
the two: fewer places used, more people left out. The threshold fixes
the trade without saying how it was valued; a budget for places would
fix it too.

| | selected | not selected |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **ill enough to need the program** | right | left out |
| **not** | a place used | right |

The offset moves the second error onto one group. For a Black patient
at the enrollment threshold, the score says "not ill enough" at a level
of illness at which it says "selected" for a White patient. The price
of an error is paid by the person it falls on, and the offset decides
who that is. The fourth lens asks who bears the error; here the answer
is the group whose costs were lower at the same need.

Then the standing question. Who benefited from that choice being
invisible? The tool predicted cost, and the authors call that choice
reasonable, since "the program's goal, at least in part, is to reduce
costs" (Obermeyer and colleagues 2019, "Problem formulation"). Nobody
had to decide that cost stood for need; the label did it for them. And
would a more competent analyst have chosen differently? The paper's own
answer is yes, in a specific way: the program mostly prevents acute
episodes in people with chronic illness, so avoidable cost or the
number of chronic conditions would have measured what the program was
for, and the authors worked with the manufacturer to change the label.

### A noisy measure flattens a slope

The first of the three routes is noise. Let $Y = Y^\star + \varepsilon$,
with $\varepsilon$ independent of $Y^\star$, mean zero and variance
$\sigma_\varepsilon^2$. The hospital has the measure and wants need.
The best linear guess of need from the measure is the regression of
$Y^\star$ on $Y$, whose slope is
$$
\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Y^\star, Y)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}
= \frac{\operatorname{Var}(Y^\star)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y^\star) + \sigma_\varepsilon^2}
= \lambda ,
$$
because $\operatorname{Cov}(Y^\star, \varepsilon) = 0$. The factor
$\lambda$ is between $0$ and $1$ and is called the **reliability** of
the measure: the share of its variance that is need rather than noise.
When $Y^\star$ and $\varepsilon$ are jointly normal with mean zero the
regression is the conditional mean,
$$
E[Y^\star \mid Y = y] = \lambda y .
$$


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```
`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'
```


:::

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](notes_files/figure-html/attenuation-1.png){fig-alt='A scatterplot of need against the noisy measure, with the fitted line of slope one half flatter than the dashed identity line.' width=528}
:::
:::


The figure has $\operatorname{Var}(Y^\star) = \sigma_\varepsilon^2 = 1$,
so $\lambda = 1/2$. A patient whose measure is two units above average
is expected to be one unit above average in need (the measure has a
larger standard deviation than need, so in each variable's own standard
deviations the shrinkage is by $\sqrt{\lambda}$). Selecting the top 3%
by the measure selects people whose need is high, but less high than
their measure says, by the factor $\lambda$. Manheim and Garrabrant
call this the regressional version of Goodhart's law: pick the largest
values of a proxy and you have picked its noise along with its signal.
The slope is **attenuated** toward zero by $\lambda$, however large the
sample. This is week 2's sentence again, more data, the same wrong
answer, with variance in the measure turned into bias in the slope.

### Noise and an omitted variable

The slope above has need on the left. In a regression course the noisy
measure is usually on the right, as the predictor, and often something
is left out as well. Does care improve health? In this subsection $Y$
is an outcome, not the measure of need. Let $Y$ be a person's health
next year, $X^\star$ the number of times they saw a doctor this
year, and $X = X^\star + \varepsilon$ the number they report, with
$\varepsilon$ independent of everything else. Let $Z$ be how ill they
were this year, which is not in the data, and
$$
Y = \beta X^\star + \gamma Z + U ,
$$
with $U$ independent of $X^\star$, $Z$ and $\varepsilon$. Someone with
data on $X$ and $Y$ regresses health on reported visits. The population
slope is
$$
\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X, Y)}{\operatorname{Var}(X)}
= \frac{\beta \operatorname{Var}(X^\star) + \gamma \operatorname{Cov}(X^\star, Z)}{\operatorname{Var}(X^\star) + \sigma_\varepsilon^2}
= \lambda\,(\beta + \gamma\delta),
\qquad
\delta = \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X^\star, Z)}{\operatorname{Var}(X^\star)} ,
$$
where $\lambda$ is the reliability of the report and $\delta$ is the
slope of illness on visits. With $\gamma = 0$ this is $\beta\lambda$,
attenuation alone. With no noise, $\lambda = 1$, it is last week's slope
with a variable left out, $\beta + \gamma\delta$, whose bias is
$\gamma\delta$.

The two biases work differently. Noise multiplies the slope by
$\lambda$, which is between 0 and 1: it pulls the slope toward zero and
never changes its sign. The left-out variable adds $\gamma\delta$ to
$\beta$ inside the bracket. Its sign is the sign of the product of the
two arrows out of $Z$, and it can change the sign of the slope. Visits help, $\beta > 0$. The ill visit more,
$\delta > 0$, and are less healthy next year, $\gamma < 0$, so
$\gamma\delta < 0$. If $\gamma\delta < -\beta$, the people who visit
more are less healthy next year, the slope is negative, and the data
say that care does harm. Noise only shrinks that wrong answer toward
zero.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](notes_files/figure-html/noise_ovb-1.png){fig-alt='The slope of health on reported visits against lambda, from 0 to 1, for three values of gamma times delta with beta equal to one half. With gamma delta 0.25 the line rises to 0.75 and crosses beta at lambda two thirds; with minus 0.25 it rises to 0.25, below beta; with minus 1 it falls to minus 0.5, below zero for every lambda.' width=624}
:::
:::


The figure has $\beta = 1/2$. When $\gamma\delta > 0$ the two biases
pull against each other, and the slope can be too large or too small:
it is larger than $\beta$ when $\gamma\delta > \beta(1 - \lambda)/\lambda$.
The classic case is the return to a year of schooling, with earnings
for health, years of schooling for visits and ability left out. Ability
is usually taken to raise both schooling and earnings, so
$\gamma\delta > 0$. Card (1999, section 3.3 and the abstract) reviews the evidence: the
reliability of self-reported schooling is about 0.9, and studies of
identical twins suggest a small upward bias from ability, so the two
partly offset.

None of $\lambda$, $\gamma$ and $\delta$ comes from the data on $X$
and $Y$. The reliability needs a second report of the same quantity,
and the term for the left-out variable needs a measure of it or a
design that holds it fixed. From $X$ and $Y$ alone you cannot tell
whether the slope is too large, too small or of the wrong sign.

This is classical noise, independent of everything else. Noise that is
related to the true value, to the outcome or to the left-out variable
can move the slope in either direction, and so can noise in a variable
that is adjusted for, which leaves part of the confounding it was meant
to remove. Noise in the outcome is different again: it goes into $U$,
widens the interval around the slope and leaves its center alone.

### Need, resources and care-seeking

The hospital selected on cost and wanted need, and the model so far
has cost differ from need by an offset and by noise. Cost also depends
on other things about a person. Write
$$
Y = Y^\star + W + C + \varepsilon ,
$$
where $W$ stands for a person's resources (insurance that pays, income,
transport, time off work, a doctor who records every diagnosis), what
turns need into care and care into cost, and $C$ for care-seeking, how
readily a person goes to a doctor at a given level of need. The noise
$\varepsilon$ is the rest: an accident, a test that had to be repeated.
Suppose the four are independent and normal with mean zero.

The best guess of each part from the measure is the calculation that
gave $\lambda$. For need, $\operatorname{Cov}(Y^\star, Y) = \operatorname{Var}(Y^\star)$,
so
$$
E[Y^\star \mid Y = y] = \frac{\operatorname{Var}(Y^\star)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}\, y ,
$$
and likewise for $W$, $C$ and $\varepsilon$. The four fractions add up
to 1, because $\operatorname{Var}(Y)$ is the sum of the four variances.
Averaging over the people selected, those with $Y > t$, gives each
part's mean among them: its share of $\operatorname{Var}(Y)$ times
their mean cost,
$$
E[Y^\star \mid Y > t] = E\big[E[Y^\star \mid Y] \,\big|\, Y > t\big]
= \frac{\operatorname{Var}(Y^\star)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}\, E[Y \mid Y > t] .
$$
With variances 1, 1/2, 1/4 and 1/4, the shares are 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 and
1/8. Of the selected's mean cost above the population mean, half is
need, a quarter resources, an eighth care-seeking and an eighth noise.
The selected are a mixture: some are there mostly because they are
ill, some because they could turn need into care, some because they
seek care readily.

Two more things follow. Among the selected the parts are negatively
related, although they are independent in the population: to clear the
threshold with less need, a person needed more of something else. And
when the parts are related in the population, the mixture changes. If
poorer people are sicker, with the spread of need unchanged, the sickest have fewer resources and generate
less cost than their need, and the places go less to need: the
hospital's offset again, inside one group.

Some of the parts are more under a person's control than others. How
readily someone seeks care is partly a choice. Illness, income and
where someone lives are much less so. The ability to raise a score
without raising what it stands for, gaming in the section on systems
that adapt below, is often a resource. A program that selects on the
score rewards all of these together.

## Reinforcement learning

**Notation:** this section uses the letters of reinforcement learning:
$S$ state, $A$ action, $R$ reward, $\pi$ policy, $U$ utility.

An agent observes a **state** $S$, takes an **action** $A$, and receives
a **reward** $R$. A **policy** $\pi$ is a rule that chooses the action
from the state, $A = \pi(S)$, and learning means changing the policy to
make the expected reward, $E_\pi[R]$, large, where $E_\pi$ is the
expectation when the agent acts by $\pi$. The **utility** $U$ is what
we care about. A utilitarian would choose the policy whose
expected utility $E_\pi[U]$ is largest. The agent is given $R$ instead,
because $R$ can be measured and $U$ often cannot: in the job center
below, $U$ needs what would have happened without the course. $R$ and
$U$ can come apart. In the letters of the rest of these notes, $R$ is
$Y$ and $U$ is $Y^\star$.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](notes_files/figure-html/rl_loop-1.png){fig-alt='A loop: the agent, with policy pi, sends an action A to the environment, which returns a state S and a reward R to the agent.' width=576}
:::
:::


Amodei and colleagues (2016) use a cleaning robot as a running example.
In these letters, the state is what the robot's camera shows, the
actions are where to move and whether to clean, and the utility is a
clean room. If the reward is for not seeing any mess, the robot can
earn it by closing its eyes, or by covering the mess with something it
cannot see through.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](notes_files/figure-html/robot-1.png){fig-alt='Three rooms, each earning reward 1. Left: the robot cleans, and its view shows no mess. Middle: it closes its eyes, and the mess stays. Right: it covers the mess, which stays under the cover.' width=672}
:::
:::


Now a variant of week 3's job center, with 100 places on the course,
which helps some people more than others. Take the rates that follow as
what would happen under assignment to the course or to no course, so
that the differences are effects and not last week's confounded
comparison. Of people who worked last year, 70% are in work six months
later if they take the course and 64% if they do not; of people who
did not work last year, 40% and 14%. The
state is a person's record, the action is to refer or not, and the
center is judged on the share of the people it refers who are in work,
its placement rate. That rate is its reward. Referring 100 people who
worked last year earns a rate of 70% and puts 6 more people in work,
on average, than would be in work without the course. Referring 100
who did not earns 40% and puts 26 more in work. A center judged on its
placement rate refers the first group; a utilitarian counting the jobs
the course creates refers the second, and so serves the people who
need the course most.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](notes_files/figure-html/skim-1.png){fig-alt='Two panels of invented numbers for the variant job center. Placement rate: 70 percent if it sends people who worked last year, 40 percent if it sends those who did not. Extra people in work: 6 against 26.' width=576}
:::
:::


Choosing people who would have done well anyway is called cream
skimming. Heckman, Heinrich and Smith (2002) studied it in US
job-training centers funded under the Job Training Partnership Act,
which were judged partly on employment rates. They found the short-run
measures "weakly, and sometimes perversely, related to long run
impacts." They also found that cream skimming made little difference
to the programs' efficiency, in either direction, unlike the invented
numbers above, and concluded: "Opposition to cream skimming must come
on equity grounds." Equity here is about who is served; efficiency is
about the total.

The job center chose between two utilities, and the hospital faces the
same choice. Its program, the paper says, mostly prevents acute
episodes in people with chronic illness. One candidate for $U$ is how
ill a patient is; another is how much the extra care would help them.
They pick out different people whenever the care helps some patients
more than others, which is the heterogeneity last week's average
treatment effect averaged over. Telling the two apart needs an
estimate of the program's effect on each kind of patient, a causal
claim that the hospital's data, on patients it chose to enroll, do not
give by themselves. Choosing between them is not an estimate at all:
it is a judgment about whose good the program is for, and no label
makes it for you.

Each of the four difficulties of utilitarianism from week 3 becomes a
choice someone makes in building such an agent. Defining utility
becomes choosing $R$, a measurable stand-in for $U$, and in both
examples the two come apart. Trading off between people becomes adding
the reward up over the people the agent serves; the placement rate
counts only the people referred. Judging acts or rules becomes
choosing a policy, a rule that treats alike everyone in the same
state. Judging each action on its own and judging the rule can give
different answers: when a rule has to treat different situations
alike, as a model that sees only a few variables about each person
does; when places are limited, so that one referral uses a place
another person could have had; and when people respond to the rule
itself. Predicting consequences becomes choosing a model of what the
actions do, which is a causal model.

Is $E_\pi[U]$ a causal quantity? It can be read as one, the expected
utility if the agent's actions were set by $\pi$, but that reading
needs assumptions beyond last week's. An intervention in last week's
sense sets a variable for everyone in a population. Here one agent
follows a rule. The people and systems it acts on may respond to what
it does, sometimes adversarially, and what happens to one of them can
depend on what was done to others. Causal reinforcement learning, a
subfield surveyed by Deng, Jiang, Long and Zhang (2023), brings causal
models into reinforcement learning.

These letters clash with the ones used for prediction, which most of
the course uses.

| | prediction | reinforcement learning |
|:---|:---|:---|
| $A$ | sensitive attribute: something a person *is* | action: something an agent *does* |
| $R$ | risk score, with $\hat Y = 1\{R \ge t\}$ | reward |
| $U$ | unobserved variable | utility |
| $S$, $\pi$ | not used | state, policy |

If you read about reinforcement learning you will meet these letters
with these meanings. New letters invented for this course would teach a
convention nobody else uses. Two rules are enough. Material that uses
the reinforcement-learning letters says so in one line at the top, as
this section does. And the two sets of letters are never mixed inside
one diagram or one derivation. A classifier described as an agent takes
its prediction $\hat Y$ as its action, which reinforcement learning
would write as $A$. Mixing the two there would give $A$ two meanings in
one line.

## Systems that adapt

### When a measure becomes a target

So far the people being measured have done nothing. Now reward the
measure. Before the rule,
$$
Y = Y^\star + \varepsilon ,
$$
and selecting the people with the highest $Y$ is **conditioning**: it
picks out a group whose need is high, shrunk by $\lambda$, because the
old relation between $Y$ and $Y^\star$ still holds among the people
picked. After the rule, each person can add an amount $g \ge 0$ to their
own $Y$, at some cost, without changing $Y^\star$:
$$
Y = Y^\star + \varepsilon + g .
$$


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](notes_files/figure-html/goodhart_dag-1.png){fig-alt='Two graphs. Before: need and noise point to the measure Y. After: a third arrow into Y, from effort chosen to raise the measure.' width=672}
:::
:::


Replacing the equation that generates $Y$ is what week 3 called an
**intervention**: a new assignment for one variable, every other line
left alone. The relation between $Y$ and $Y^\star$ that held before
the rule need not hold after it. Which people it fails for depends on
who can pay for $g$.

Who can respond decides what the response does. Compare two cases
with the same 300 places for the highest $Y$. If everyone adds the
same $1$ to their $Y$, every ranking is unchanged, the same 300 people
are selected, and nothing about them has changed: a rewarded measure
is not spoiled by the reward alone. If half of the people are able to
add $1$ and the rest cannot, the ranking changes, and it changes toward
the people who could respond. The simulation below has ten thousand
people, need and noise standard normal, and who is able to add $1$
unrelated to need. Each panel plots the measure against need, with the
cutoff for 300 places dashed and the 300 selected drawn solid. The
first two panels are the same picture shifted up by one: the same
people are selected. In the third the 300 places go mostly to people
who were able to add $1$, and the selected reach further down in need.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](notes_files/figure-html/goodhart_sim-1.png){fig-alt='Three scatterplots of the measure Y against need Y*, with the cutoff for 300 places dashed and the selected drawn solid. Before the rule and after everyone adds 1 the same people are selected; after half are able to add 1, the selected are mostly those able, reaching lower need.' width=720}
:::
:::


The fall in mean need in the third case is modest, because the people
able to add $1$ were drawn from the same need distribution as everyone
else; what changes most is who the places go to. The first two cases
select the same people, which is the check that it is the difference
in response, not the response itself, that moves the allocation. In the paper's setting the equivalent
would be a hospital that rewards patients, or their doctors, for a high
score, after which the score measures who responded to the reward.

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

```

Two formal versions of a system that adapts are in the reading's
authors' own work.

**Strategic classification** (Hardt, Megiddo, Papadimitriou and
Wootters 2016). A classifier is published. Each person then changes
their features, at a cost that depends on the change, to get the label
they want. The classifier is scored on the features as changed, against
each person's true label, which is fixed by the features as they were
before the change; so every response is gaming, and the
design problem is a classifier that stays accurate when everyone games
it. The paper gives efficient algorithms for a natural class of cost
functions and shows the general problem is hard.

**Performative prediction** (Perdomo, Zrnic, Mendler-Dünner and Hardt
2020). A prediction that is acted on can change the thing it predicts:
a traffic forecast changes which roads people take, and a forecast that
a loan will default can make it default. The authors call such
predictions performative. The distribution the model is evaluated on
depends on the model deployed, by whatever mechanism, and the labels
can move along with the features. The question is what retraining on
the data a model induces converges to, a model they call
performatively stable, and whether that point has low loss. They give
conditions under which it does, and show that strategic classification
is the special case in which the mechanism is individuals responding to
a published rule.

**Gaming and improvement.** Miller, Milli and Hardt (2020) separate
responses to a rule that game it from responses that improve what it
stands for, and show that designing a rule that rewards improvement
"must inevitably solve a non-trivial causal inference problem." The
example here is ours. Take a course judged by its students' test
scores. Practicing raises skill, and skill
raises the score; memorizing old papers raises the score without
touching skill. Each graph is a claim someone could dispute.


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](notes_files/figure-html/gaming_graphs-1.png){fig-alt='Two graphs. Improvement: practice points to skill, which points to test score. Gaming: memorizing old papers points straight to test score, beside the arrow from skill.' width=672}
:::
:::


Whether a response to a rule is gaming or improvement depends on the
causal model. If the feature a person changes raises the outcome, the change
is improvement, and $Y^\star$ rises with $Y$; if it changes only the
measure, the change is gaming, as in the second graph. The graph says
which features can affect the outcome at all; whether a given change
raises it, and by how much, needs the model's equations too. A rule meant
to reward improvement has to know which, and that is a causal inference
problem; the authors show that any procedure for designing such rules
has to solve one. Conditioning is not intervening, a third time: the
rule intervenes on the people it is applied to, and what they do in
response is decided by the graph, not by the rule's intentions.

### Engagement

**Notation:** this section uses the letters of reinforcement learning:
$S$ state, $A$ action, $R$ reward, $\pi$ policy, $U$ utility.

A recommender system is an agent. Its state is what it knows about a
user, its action is what to show next, and its reward is whatever the
platform can measure about the response: a click, a view, time
watched, a share. In August 2012 YouTube told its creators that its
discovery features had been "designed to drive views," which rewarded
videos that got clicked over videos that kept viewers watching, and
that it would rank by watch time instead. A platform's reward is
engagement in some form. A user's utility is something else: being
informed, or entertained, on their own terms, and not manipulated.
The two need not conflict: a change that keeps viewers watching can
serve them too. Where they do conflict, where raising $U$ would lower
$R$, a platform whose revenue rises with $R$ has a reason not to, and
nobody inside has to decide to leave the gap open; the reward decides
for them. The post describes one change of reward, not the incentives
behind it; that reading is mine. Last week's lens
asked which comparison gets reported; this week's asks what is being
optimized, and for whom.

Week 2 showed the selection half of this story: a feed surfaces the
most extreme of $n$ items. This is the optimization half: a feed that
ranks by $R$ changes what gets made, because the people who make it
write for the score.

## Lenses

What are we optimizing or predicting? Cost, standing in for need.
Citations, standing in for a contribution. A placement rate, standing
in for jobs created. Views, or watch time, standing in for a viewer's
good. In each case the first word is what the system can measure and
the second is what someone wanted; the system's designer chose the
first and the system optimized it.

Who bears the error? A threshold at the 97th percentile makes two
errors, a place used on someone who did not need it and a person left
out who did, and trades them against each other, whether by a judgment
about their costs or by how many places the program has. An offset in the
measure moves the second error onto one group, the one whose costs
were lower at the same need. The cleaning robot's owner bears the
difference between the robot's reward and a clean room; the job
seekers a center did not refer bear the difference between its
placement rate and the jobs the course would have created.

What can be changed, and how? What things are considered "controlled
for" or "held fixed," and is that realistic? This lens is new this
week, and it is last week's method put as a question. Benefit is an
effect: it compares the same patient with the extra care and without
it, holding the patient fixed. A slope of health on reported visits
is read as the effect of a visit with illness held fixed; illness is not
in the data, so nothing held it fixed. The lens also asks what the
people scored can change: how readily they seek care is easier for them
to change than how ill they are. Goodhart's law is the case where something was assumed to stay
fixed and did not: a rule rewarding the score assumed that the
relation between the score and need would hold, and the people scored
changed it. Strategic classification holds the true label fixed while
people change their features; performative prediction drops that
assumption and lets the whole distribution move.

And why? A measure is chosen because it can be measured. Cost is in
the billing system and need is not. Views are counted and a viewer's
understanding is not. The choice is made once, often by a vendor, and
afterward nobody has to make it again; the score makes it for them.

### Exercises, problems and simulation

The exercises, done on students' own time, compute who is selected
under an offset at a new threshold and with a fixed number of places,
derive $\lambda$ from the covariance algebra above, then the slope
$\lambda(\beta + \gamma\delta)$ with numbers that make it too large,
too small and of the wrong sign, and simulate it. In class, problem 1
draws the graph of need, resources and care-seeking with selection on
cost and computes each part's mean among the selected, and the class
simulates the selection, with gaming that depends on resources.
Problem 2 changes the label to the number of active chronic conditions
and asks what reaches it and what happens once it is paid on.
